meaning: Let's discuss this later, with only the people who need to.
useWhen: One topic is eating up a group meeting.
example: Good point, Rahul. **Let's take this offline** after the call.
careful: Don't use it to dodge a topic. Follow up the same day.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about internet access
wrong.text: The Wi-Fi stopped. Let's take this offline.

similar: Can we pick this up after the call?

topic: Could you walk us through it?
phrase: Could you walk us through it?
meaning: Explain it step by step.
useWhen: You need to understand a process.
example: Could you walk us through it, starting with the login?
careful: Ask about a process, not someone's journey on foot.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Could you walk us through it to the station?

meaning: Return to this topic later.
useWhen: Another point needs attention first.
example: Let's come back to that after we agree on the budget.
careful: Name when you will return to the topic.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Let's come back to that yesterday.

similar: Can we return to that after lunch?

topic: Are we on the same page?
phrase: Are we on the same page?
meaning: Do we understand or agree about this?
useWhen: You want to check a shared understanding.
example: I'll book the room; you'll order lunch. Are we on the same page?
careful: Don't assume silence means agreement.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Are we on the same page? Please turn to page six.

similar: Do we agree on the plan?

meaning: Asking again about an earlier message.
useWhen: You are waiting for a reply.
example: Just following up. Can you confirm Friday's booking?
careful: Mention the request; repeated reminders can feel pushy.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Just following up. Nice to meet you for the first time.

similar: Any update on my earlier message?
Have you had a chance to check?

meaning: Here is information you may need later.
useWhen: You are sharing useful background.
example: For your reference, the receipt is attached.
careful: State any action separately; this phrase doesn't request one.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: For your reference, approve this immediately.

similar: In case you need it later.

meaning: Thanks for warning or telling me early.
useWhen: Someone tells you about a change.
example: The train is delayed? Thanks for the heads-up.
careful: Use with familiar colleagues; formal emails may need plainer thanks.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Thanks for the heads-up. I love your new haircut.

meaning: I understand your reason.
useWhen: You want to acknowledge a view before responding.
example: I see your point. I'd still prefer the earlier train.
careful: Understanding isn't agreement; explain your own view next.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: I see your point, so I automatically agree.

similar: I can see why you think that.

topic: I'm not sure that will work.
phrase: I'm not sure that will work.
meaning: I have doubts about this plan.
useWhen: You need to raise a concern gently.
example: I'm not sure that will work. The shop closes at six.
careful: Add a reason so the other person can respond.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: I'm not sure that will work. It definitely works perfectly.

similar: I have a concern about that.

meaning: Could we both give up something to agree?
useWhen: You want a compromise.
example: You want six; I want eight. Could we meet halfway at seven?
careful: This asks for a compromise, which may not be possible.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Could we meet halfway? Only you must change.

similar: Could we both adjust a little?

meaning: You dealt with a situation effectively.
useWhen: Someone managed a difficult moment.
example: That call was tense. You handled that well.
careful: Say what they did well; avoid sounding surprised.

wrong.label: ✗ Sounds surprised
wrong.text: Wow, you actually handled that well!

similar: You did a great job with that.

meaning: That had a useful, noticeable effect.
useWhen: You want to show why help mattered.
example: Thanks for checking the numbers. That made a real difference.
careful: Name the effect when it is not obvious.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: That made a real difference. Nothing changed at all.

topic: Thanks for going the extra mile.
phrase: Thanks for going the extra mile.
meaning: Thanks for doing more than expected.
useWhen: Someone made an additional effort.
example: You stayed to help clean up. Thanks for going the extra mile.
careful: Don't use praise to demand unpaid extra work.

wrong.label: ✗ Not to ask for more
wrong.text: Thanks for going the extra mile. Can you work Sunday too?

topic: What's the latest we can leave?
phrase: What's the latest we can leave?
meaning: When must we leave to be on time?
useWhen: You need a departure deadline.
example: Dinner starts at eight. What's the latest we can leave?
careful: Specify leave, start, or finish; the deadline must be clear.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: What's the latest we can leave? I mean when can we arrive?

similar: When do we need to leave by?

topic: Could we have a little more time?
phrase: Could we have a little more time?
meaning: Can the deadline move later?
useWhen: You need extra time to finish.
example: Could we have a little more time? I'll finish by tomorrow morning.
careful: Offer a specific new time instead of leaving it open.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Could we have a little more time? I mean less time.

meaning: We are progressing as planned.
useWhen: You are giving a progress update.
example: The bags are packed. We're on track to leave at six.
careful: Use only if the planned result still looks achievable.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: We're on track. We will definitely miss our deadline.

meaning: We are later than planned.
useWhen: You need to flag a delay.
example: We're running behind. Can you tell them we'll arrive at seven?
careful: Give a new estimate when you can.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: We're running behind. We finished early.

meaning: Decide as things happen.
useWhen: You cannot make a firm plan yet.
example: If the rain stops, we'll go out. Let's play it by ear.
careful: Avoid this when someone needs a firm commitment.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Let's play it by ear. Every detail is fixed.

meaning: We share the same difficult situation.
useWhen: You want someone to feel less alone.
example: You haven't found a flat either? We're in the same boat.
careful: Use for a shared difficulty, not just any similarity.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: You're struggling; everything is easy for me. We're in the same boat.

similar: We're dealing with the same problem.
I am in that situation too.

meaning: Let's stop working for today.
useWhen: You have done enough for now.
example: We've packed all the books. Let's call it a day.
careful: This ends the activity for today; it is not a short break.

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong use
wrong.text: Let's call it a day and restart in five minutes.

similar: We can finish the rest tomorrow.
